brief: Tonight is Pull B, and it is your first session back after three days off — you last trained Monday. Nothing in your log says why, and I am not going to guess. If you were run down or away, treat tonight as a re-entry and the bottom of every rep range is a pass. If you simply missed the window, you are rested, and this is a good night to push. The big change is the bent-over row. Last Pull B you finished ten reps on 115, then 135, then 145, and only then came up one short at the top — nine at 150 instead of ten. Three of those four sets had stopped asking you for anything, and they are what ate the last one. So the ramp gets shorter and heavier and then stops: 125 for eight, 140 for eight, and 150 for ten, twice. You reach the top set having done a lot less work than last time, which is the entire point of the change. If the second set of 150 only gives you eight, that is still inside the range and still the best you have done on this lift. Close-grip pulldown goes to 127.5. You took 120 for a clean ten on all three sets last time, and this is not new ground — you pulled 127.5 for all three sets on four separate nights in January and February. Incline curls are the awkward one: the rack has nothing between 25 and 30, and you have finished one rep short on the third set at 25 two sessions running. So take the 30 on the first set only, for eight, then drop to 25 for two sets of ten. Taking a new dumbbell on the freshest set is the only way across a gap that size. Shrugs stay at 70, but the card asks 15, 14, 14 — one more rep on every set than last time. The next dumbbell is 80 and there is nothing in between, so reps are the only currency you have here. Cable reverse curl comes down to 35: at 37.5 your reps ran 12, 11, 10, and this slot asks for at least twelve, so the weight is wrong, not your effort. Straight-arm pulldown holds at 37.5 for 13, 13, 12. On the day, rest a full three minutes on the row and about seventy-five seconds on everything after the pulldown. One last thing, and it is not a lift: you have one bodyweight reading since 4 January — 206 lb on 21 July — and one cardio session in the entire log, also 21 July. You are just under thirty weeks from the show. Standing on a scale this morning would be worth more to March than any weight on tonight's card.

flags.note: No session logged on 4, 5 or 6 August — the longest break in this block. Tonight's numbers are built on your 3 August data, because that is the last thing the review can see.

Your 3 August session was the shortest of the block at 42 minutes and its main press stored no sets, and then came three days off. That may mean you were run down, or it may mean the machine was busy and you were in a hurry. Your trainers cannot tell from the log, and only you can.

Monday's Arnold presses are still not in your log — the overhead press slot stored zero sets when you swapped the exercise, so that work cannot move the slot. Logging substitutes under the slot they replace is what keeps them counting.
One bodyweight reading since 4 January (206 lb on 21 July) and one cardio session in the whole log. With just under thirty weeks to the show, that is the thinnest part of your prep.

dissent.progression: Shorten the ramp and buy a second set at the top — 125 and 140 for eight, then 150 for ten twice.
dissent.recovery: Heaviest axial load on the first night back after the longest layoff of the block: repeat 28 July exactly, 115, 135, 145 for ten and 150 for nine.
dissent.why: Recovery's argument is that the top set was already at its ceiling, and that is true — but its own prescription asks for 150x9, which is the rep he already did, so on its own terms nothing could ever earn the jump it says it is protecting. Progression's plan is also the one that actually answers recovery's concern: 125x8 and 140x8 is a little over half the ramp work of 115x10, 135x10 and 145x10, so he reaches 150 substantially fresher than he did on 28 July, which is when the tenth rep got away from him. Three days of rest with no pain note, no injury and no measured rest drift is not a reason to prescribe a night he has already had. I checked the brake's own file for grounds to hold and it recorded no veto and no fatigue signal.

dissent.progression: Hold 70 but ask for 15, 14, 14 — one more rep on every set.
dissent.recovery: Hold 70 at 14, 13, 13 — he is improving, but the next dumbbell is 80 and the first night back is the wrong time for a fourteen percent jump.
dissent.why: Both seats agree the weight stays at 70 and both agree the 80s are not earned yet, so the only question is what the card asks for. Recovery's 14, 13, 13 is exactly what he logged on 28 July, and a card that asks for the night you already had cannot move anything — he would arrive at the next Pull B in the same place, which is precisely the silent copy-paste this panel exists to catch. Progression's 15, 14, 14 is one rep per set and puts the top of the rep range on the board for the first time, which is the only thing that ever buys the 80s.

dissent.progression: Take 30 for eight on the freshest set, then 25 for two sets of ten.
dissent.recovery: Hold 25 at 10, 10, 9 — the third set keeps falling short, so 25 is not finished, and 30 is a twenty percent jump.
dissent.why: Recovery names the right standard and then does not prescribe it: it argues the raise should wait for three clean sets of ten at 25, and then writes a card asking for nine on the third set. Asking for the shortfall guarantees the shortfall. Progression's descending order is the honest answer to a rack with nothing between 25 and 30 — the new dumbbell gets the one set where he is fresh, at eight reps, which is the bottom of the range and the correct place to meet a weight for the first time, and the remaining volume still happens at 25. This risks one set, not the lift.

dissent.progression: Cut to 35 for 13, 12, 12 — 37.5 is decaying and 35 is the loadable notch below it.
dissent.recovery: Hold 37.5 at 12, 11, 10 — two sessions is thin evidence and holding a reverse curl for one night costs nothing.
dissent.why: Holding costs nothing only if the card is honest, and recovery's card is not: this slot asks for at least twelve reps and its prescription writes in an eleven and a ten, so it puts numbers below the slot's own floor on screen and calls that a hold. The lift went 12, 12, 12 at 37.5 on 21 July and 12, 11, 10 on 28 July, which is the one thing on this day moving backwards. 35 is real on his machine — the 32.5 pin with both 1.25 add-ons — and it is the same weight this panel ruled for yesterday, so nothing is being reversed.

proposals.why: Straight-arm pulldown asks twelve to fifteen and your last two Pull B nights at 37.5 landed on 13, 11, 12 and 13, 12, 12 — never the fifteen it wants, so the weight can never move. This is the same trap you cleared on the close-grip pulldown on 3 August: ask ten to twelve, and the twelves you already do earn the next step.

Push A's rope pushdown asks ten to twelve and your six sets there came in at eight, seven, nine and eight, seven, eight — never once inside the range — while the same job on Push B asks twelve to fifteen and lands at fifteen and fourteen with the weight climbing, so this gives Push A the range that already works on the other day.

The split squat is the only single-leg work in your week and the smallest slot in the program at two sets, against seven sets of leg press across both leg days, and you have finished both sets on every Legs A night since it was added — a third set is the only way to grow the one thing that shows a left-right difference on stage.

Still open from Tuesday, and now every seat agrees: Push A holds the last face pulls in your week, the ones you wrote "Do you have a brain?" next to on 31 July and skipped for angels and demons on 28 July, and this puts the reverse pec deck there instead — same back of the shoulder, and it is the machine you have carried from 82.5 to 90 without missing a set.

Still open from Tuesday, and this is not the cut to two sets you turned down on 3 August: Legs A asks for four calf sets and you have done two, two and three, and because the weight only moves when you finish every set the plan asks for, this makes the prescription the three you actually do.

overrides.reason: Last Pull B you finished ten on 115, 135 and 145 and then gave a rep back at the top — nine at 150. Those three ramp sets had stopped asking anything and they are what cost you the tenth rep, so the ramp is now shorter and heavier and stops early: 125 and 140 for eight, then two sets at 150 for ten. You get to the top set much fresher than last time. Eight at 150 on the second one is still a pass.

You took 120 for a clean ten on all three sets last Pull B, and 120 has been your top set on this machine since 13 July. 127.5 is the smallest step it has, and it is not new ground — you pulled 127.5 for all three sets on four separate nights in January and February.

Two Pull B nights carrying 37.5 on all three sets — 13, 11, 12 and then 13, 12, 12. The next pin on this machine is 45, which is exactly a twenty percent jump and your log has not paid for it, so the weight holds and the middle set gets one more rep than last time.

The 70s went from 12, 12, 12 to 14, 13, 13 — moving the right way. The rack jumps straight to 80 with nothing in between, so reps are the only currency here: one more on every set, and fifteen on the first one puts the top of the range on the board for the first time.

Two sessions running you have been one rep short on the third set at 25 — eight, then nine. The rack has nothing between 25 and 30, so the 30 goes on the one set where you are fresh, for eight, which is the bottom of the range and the right place to meet a new dumbbell. Then back to 25 for two sets of ten.

At 37.5 your reps ran 12, 11, 10, and the last two are under the twelve this slot asks for — that is the weight being wrong, not your effort. 35 is a real load on this stack: the 32.5 pin with both add-on weights. The 37.5 comes back once you are finishing all three sets there.
